sections.title: Where emboli come from and who gets them

blocks.text: Most pulmonary emboli are **thrombus that has propagated from a lower-limb DVT**, usually in the proximal (popliteal, femoral and iliac) or pelvic veins. Clots confined to the calf seldom embolise, but about a third extend upwards. A clot lodged in a pulmonary artery raises pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular pressure, so a large one causes **acute right heart failure (acute cor pulmonale)**. The lung beyond it is ventilated but not perfused (**dead space**); the resulting hypoxaemia drives tachypnoea.

blocks.title: Rare non-thrombotic emboli
items: **Septic** emboli from right-sided (tricuspid or pulmonary valve) endocarditis
**Tumour** emboli, classically choriocarcinoma
**Fat** after a long-bone fracture such as the femur: breathlessness, confusion and a petechial rash within days
**Air** embolism
**Amniotic fluid**, entering the maternal circulation after delivery

blocks.title: Virchow's triad applied to venous thrombosis
rows: Surgery, bed rest, plaster cast, pregnancy, long-haul travel
Cancer, surgery, pregnancy, oestrogen (combined pill, HRT), inherited thrombophilia

blocks.title: Risk factors for VTE (Davidson)
rows: Older age, obesity, varicose veins, previous DVT, family history of unprovoked VTE
Pregnancy and puerperium, oestrogen pill or HRT, travel over 4 hours, femoral IV drug use, surgery, acute illness
Major surgery over 30 minutes, abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery, hip or knee replacement, hip fracture
MI or heart failure, IBD, malignancy (worse on chemotherapy), nephrotic syndrome, COPD, pneumonia, stroke or paraplegia, any high-dependency admission
Polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, antithrombin / protein C / protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, PNH, myelofibrosis, antiphospholipid syndrome

blocks.text: Strength matters: **major surgery, trauma and strict bed rest** raise VTE risk 10–50-fold; pregnancy, oestrogens and most thrombophilias 3–10-fold; obesity and long-haul travel less than 3-fold.
A recognised risk factor is found in **80–90%** of PE. In an OSCE or viva, ask specifically about immobility, recent operations and long flights.

The picture depends on how many emboli there are, how big they are, where they lodge and how much **cardiorespiratory reserve** the patient has. Many PEs are clinically silent: at least a third of patients with DVT have an unnoticed PE, and about 70% of symptomatic PEs have an associated DVT that causes leg symptoms in only about a quarter.

blocks.title: Three clinical patterns
rows: Low cardiac output, acute right heart failure
Segmental artery blocked, lung infarction ± effusion
Progressive occlusion of small pulmonary vessels
Collapse or faintness, crushing central chest pain, apprehension, severe breathlessness
Tachycardia, hypotension, raised JVP, RV gallop, loud P2, severe cyanosis, poor urine output
Tachycardia, pleural rub, raised hemidiaphragm, crackles, often blood-stained effusion, low-grade fever
Few at first; later RV heave and loud P2; finally right heart failure
Low PaO2 and PaCO2, metabolic acidosis

blocks.title: How often features occur
items: **Dyspnoea** is the commonest symptom (73% in PIOPED), then pleuritic pain (66%), cough (37%) and haemoptysis (13%)
**Tachypnoea** is the commonest sign (54%), then tachycardia (24%) and a loud P2 (23%)
Only about a third have signs of DVT
Pocket Medicine quotes lower symptom rates (dyspnoea about 50%, pleuritic pain about 40%, haemoptysis about 8%)

blocks.title: Extra signs of a large embolus
items: Syncope and systolic hypotension or shock
Raised JVP, RV heave, gallop rhythm (right-sided S3), widely split second sound
Graham Steell murmur of pulmonary regurgitation
Cardiac arrest, typically **pulseless electrical activity (PEA)**

blocks.text: Pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, a pleural rub and **low-grade fever** fit pulmonary infarction just as well as pneumonia. Fever does not exclude PE.

sections.title: Differential diagnosis of the presenting features

blocks.title: Main alternatives by pattern (Davidson)
rows: Myocardial infarction, cardiac tamponade, aortic dissection; on echo, RV infarction can look similar

blocks.title: Telling the mimics apart
rows: Tearing pain going through to the back
Sharp pain that changes with posture
Consolidation or a lung edge on CXR
Asthma, COPD exacerbation, LVF, tamponade, anaphylaxis, panic
Wheeze; pink frothy sputum in pulmonary oedema; high PaO2 in hyperventilation
Bronchiectasis, carcinoma, TB, pneumonia, GPA, Goodpasture
Repeated blood-streaked sputum (carcinoma); fever, night sweats and weight loss (TB); rusty sputum (pneumococcal pneumonia); copious purulent sputum (bronchiectasis)

blocks.text: PE and **hyperventilation syndrome** both cause a respiratory alkalosis. The PaO2 separates them: **low in PE**, high in hyperventilation.
A known asthmatic with a sudden "attack" but **no wheeze**, who takes the combined pill and recently had leg fracture surgery, has all three parts of Virchow's triad. Think PE, not asthma.

More than 80% of patients investigated for VTE turn out not to have it, yet most deaths from PE follow **missed earlier warning signs** rather than sudden collapse. Keep the threshold for testing low.

sections.title: Diagnostic pathway: probability, D-dimer and imaging

blocks.text: Ask three questions: does the picture fit PE, are there risk factors, and is there a better explanation? Patients with **shock or hypotension** go straight to imaging. Everyone else gets a **clinical probability score**, then D-dimer or imaging depending on the result.

blocks.alt: Algorithm: suspected PE. If shocked, CTPA or bedside echo then reperfusion. If not, Wells score: 4 or less, do a D-dimer (normal excludes PE, raised leads to CTPA); over 4, go to CTPA. V/Q replaces CTPA in contrast allergy or renal impairment.

blocks.title: Two-level Wells score for PE
rows: PE more likely than any alternative
Immobilised 3 days or more, or surgery in last 4 weeks
Over 4 = PE likely; 4 or less = PE unlikely

blocks.title: Revised Geneva score (an alternative)
items: Age over 65 (+1); previous DVT/PE (+3); surgery or fracture within a month (+2); active cancer (+2)
Unilateral leg pain (+3); haemoptysis (+2); deep-vein tenderness with one-sided oedema (+4)
Heart rate 75–94 (+3) or 95 and above (+5)
Low 0–3, intermediate 4–10, high 11 or more; about 8% with a low score still have PE

blocks.title: D-dimer
items: Fibrin breakdown product: **sensitive (about 95%) but not specific (about 25%)**
Also raised with age, infection and sepsis, MI, heart failure, surgery, cancer and pregnancy
Useful only when PE is **unlikely**: a normal result then excludes it (failure rate under 2% at 3 months)
Age-adjusted cut-off: 500 below 50 years, **10 × age** from 50 years

blocks.text: When clinical probability is high, **do not rely on D-dimer**: image regardless, because a normal result does not make PE safe to dismiss.

blocks.title: Imaging tests
rows: First-line; shows clot extent and alternatives (consolidation, pneumothorax, dissection); sensitivity over 90%
Iodinated contrast: avoid in contrast allergy, caution if eGFR under 30; may miss far-peripheral clots
PE = perfusion defect in ventilated lung (mismatch); normal scan excludes PE; less radiation
Often non-diagnostic with chronic lung disease; less available
Proximal DVT in a suspected PE justifies treatment
Normal in about half of proven PE, so cannot exclude it
Unstable patient: dilated RV, clot in transit; detects tamponade, LV failure, dissection
Not a rule-out test in stable patients
Former gold standard; route for catheter therapy

blocks.text: Finish testing within **24 hours**. If PE imaging will take more than about **1 hour**, give a first dose of anticoagulant while waiting.
A negative CTPA in a patient with **high clinical probability** still misses about 5% of PEs. Consider leg ultrasound or a V/Q scan.

blocks.title: Pregnancy
items: VTE is the leading **direct cause of maternal death** in the UK
Compression leg ultrasound can be the first test; CTPA if it is normal
CTPA: low fetal dose (0.01–0.06 mGy) but more radiation to the breast
V/Q: higher fetal dose (0.11–0.22 mGy) but much less to the breast
Treat with LMWH; warfarin is teratogenic

blocks.note: CTPA with a saddle embolus straddling the pulmonary artery bifurcation
V/Q scan: right upper lobe perfusion is absent while ventilation is preserved (mismatch)

sections.title: Bedside tests: ECG, chest X-ray, ABG and biomarkers

blocks.title: What the first-line tests show
rows: Often normal; **sinus tachycardia** commonest; anterior T inversion; with large clots RV strain: S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis deviation, dominant R in V1, T inversion V1–V4, AF
Often normal; raised hemidiaphragm, linear atelectasis, effusion, wedge-shaped opacity, oligaemia
Low PaO2, normal or low PaCO2, raised A–a gradient, respiratory alkalosis; normal in a significant minority; metabolic acidosis in massive PE
Raised from RV stretch and injury

blocks.text: The textbook **S1Q3T3** pattern is uncommon, even in massive PE. Sinus tachycardia is the usual finding.

blocks.title: Chest X-ray signs to recognise
items: **Hampton hump**: wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity of infarction
**Westermark sign**: oligaemic, under-perfused lung beyond the clot
Raised hemidiaphragm and horizontal linear shadows at the bases
Small effusion, often blood-stained
Enlarged pulmonary artery

blocks.text: A **normal chest film in a breathless, hypoxaemic patient** should make you think of PE, as should bilateral changes in someone with one-sided pleuritic pain.
Consider PE in chest pain with a **raised troponin**. The rise reflects RV ischaemia and predicts a worse outcome.

blocks.note: Chest X-ray features of thromboembolism and infarction: wedge opacity, raised diaphragm, linear shadows, effusion, oligaemia, big pulmonary artery
ECG of acute PE: S1Q3T3, sinus tachycardia at 160/min and incomplete RBBB

blocks.text: The first split is **high risk vs not high risk**, decided by haemodynamics. High-risk ("massive") PE means cardiac arrest, obstructive shock or persistent hypotension: systolic BP **below 90 mmHg** or a fall of more than 40 mmHg for over 15 minutes not explained by arrhythmia, hypovolaemia or sepsis.

blocks.title: Simplified PESI (1 point each)
rows: Chronic heart failure or lung disease

blocks.title: ESC risk classes
rows: Normotensive, sPESI 1 or more, **both** RV dysfunction and raised troponin
sPESI 1 or more, one or neither marker
Stable, sPESI 0, normal RV and troponin

blocks.title: Markers of RV strain
items: Echo: dilated, hypokinetic RV
CT: RV/LV diameter ratio over 0.9
Biomarkers: troponin and BNP

blocks.text: Early death is most likely with **echo RV dysfunction or cardiogenic shock**, and the risk falls quickly once anticoagulation starts.
Low-risk PE (sPESI 0) can be managed as an **outpatient or discharged after 24–48 hours**; higher-risk patients need admission, close observation and oxygen.

sections.title: Acute management: resuscitation, reperfusion and filters

blocks.title: General measures
items: Oxygen to keep **SaO2 above 90%**; intubate if respiratory failure
Shock: **IV fluids** to raise filling pressure; inotropes add little because the dilated RV is already maximally driven
**Avoid diuretics and vasodilators**: they lower cardiac output
Opiates (e.g. IV morphine) for pain and distress, used cautiously
Hypotensive patients: ICU, IV unfractionated heparin, vasopressors if needed
In the moribund patient, chest compressions may break up a large central clot

blocks.title: Thrombolysis
rows: No shock but RV dilatation and hypokinesis, or severe hypoxaemia
In high-risk PE, death and recurrence each fall by about half
Intracranial haemorrhage about 2% (up to 5%); screen bleeding risk first
Alteplase 10 mg IV over 1–2 minutes, then 90 mg over 2 hours (max 1.5 mg/kg if under 65 kg)
Lower dose into the clot, fewer systemic effects

blocks.title: Contraindications to fibrinolysis
items: GI or genitourinary bleeding within 21 days
Major trauma, surgery or head injury within 14 days
Recent stroke, intracranial aneurysm, aortic dissection
BP over 180/110 mmHg
Bleeding disorder, INR over 1.7 on warfarin
Pregnancy or recent delivery

blocks.title: When lysis cannot be used
items: **Surgical embolectomy**: massive PE with lysis contraindicated or failed; can save life but carries high mortality
Catheter clot fragmentation or extraction in specialist centres

blocks.title: IVC filter
items: Davidson indications: anticoagulation contraindicated, massive bleeding on anticoagulation, or **recurrent VTE despite anticoagulation**
Use a retrievable filter and remove it once anticoagulation is safely under way
Does not reduce recurrent PE compared with anticoagulation alone and raises the DVT risk
Complications: migration, IVC wall perforation, filter thrombosis with IVC obstruction

blocks.text: Sources disagree on **normotensive PE with RV strain**. Davidson allows lysis to be considered with RV dilatation or severe hypoxaemia; Kumar calls it controversial; Pocket notes less decompensation but more bleeding. Exam answer: lysis is **indicated only with shock**, and merely considered otherwise.

Anticoagulation is the **mainstay** of treatment. It stops clot extension and recurrence but does not dissolve existing thrombus. Start a treatment dose as soon as PE is suspected if imaging is delayed; do not wait for confirmation.

blocks.title: Starting regimens
rows: LMWH for at least 5 days alongside warfarin
Stop LMWH when INR is over 2 (2 days in a row); target INR **2.5 (2–3)**
Higher dose for the first **21 days**
Higher dose for the first **7 days**
After at least 5 days of LMWH
Bolus then infusion, titrated to APTT
Unstable patients or when lysis is being considered

blocks.title: Special situations
rows: LMWH; warfarin causes embryopathy at 6–12 weeks, DOACs cross the placenta
LMWH (fewer recurrences than warfarin); DOACs are an option but bleed more
Severe renal impairment or antiphospholipid syndrome
Warfarin; avoid DOACs if CrCl under 30

blocks.title: How long?
rows: At least 3 months, then usually long-term (NICE: offer long-term after unprovoked PE)
Long-term while the risk lasts; at least 6 months in cancer

blocks.title: Adverse effects
items: All agents cut recurrence by 80–90% but cause major bleeding in **1–3% per year**
Heparin: bleeding, **HIT** at 5–14 days (check platelets if given over 5 days; stop if the count halves), hyperkalaemia, osteoporosis with long use
Warfarin: slow onset (48–72 h), skin necrosis in protein C or S deficiency, teratogenic; intracerebral haemorrhage is the commonest fatal bleed
DOACs: more GI bleeding but less intracranial bleeding than warfarin

blocks.title: Warfarin reversal
items: Major bleeding: stop warfarin, give IV vitamin K 5 mg plus prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP)
INR over 8 with no or minor bleeding: stop warfarin and give vitamin K

blocks.text: Durations differ between books: Davidson gives 6 weeks to 6 months as the initial period, with 3 months for provoked VTE; Kumar says at least 3 months for any proximal DVT or PE. Davidson adds that treating beyond 6 months does not change the recurrence rate once the drug stops.

Recurrence after stopping is about **2–3%/year** after provoked VTE but **7–10%/year** after unprovoked VTE. The strongest predictors are **male sex** and a **positive D-dimer one month after stopping**.

blocks.title: Acute complications
items: Acute right heart failure with obstructive shock
Cardiac arrest, usually PEA
Pulmonary infarction with haemoptysis and a blood-stained exudative effusion

blocks.title: Later complications
items: **Recurrence**: highest in the first 6–12 months; about a third recur within 10 years

**Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)**: incomplete clot resolution leaves up to 5% persistently breathless; confirmed with perfusion scan, CTPA and echo; some are cured by **pulmonary endarterectomy**
**Post-thrombotic syndrome** of the leg after proximal DVT: swelling, heaviness, ulcers near the medial malleolus
Treatment harms: bleeding, HIT, IVC filter problems
Hidden cancer: up to 5% with unprovoked VTE are found to have cancer within a year; age-appropriate screening is enough

blocks.text: Numbers vary by book. **Post-thrombotic syndrome**: about 30% after proximal DVT in Davidson, 40% in Kumar, 23–60% in Pocket. **CTEPH**: up to 5% (Kumar) vs 2–3% (Pocket). Quote Davidson where it gives a figure.

cards.front: Commonest source of a pulmonary embolus?
cards.back: Thrombus propagating from a **lower-limb DVT** (proximal leg or pelvic veins)

cards.front: Name four non-thrombotic causes of pulmonary embolism.
cards.back: Septic (right-sided endocarditis), tumour (choriocarcinoma), fat (long-bone fracture), air, amniotic fluid

cards.front: Commonest symptom and commonest sign of PE?
cards.back: Symptom: **dyspnoea**. Sign: **tachypnoea**

cards.front: Typical cardiac arrest rhythm in massive PE?
cards.back: **Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)**

cards.front: Davidson's three key differentials for acute massive PE?
cards.back: Myocardial infarction, cardiac tamponade, aortic dissection

cards.front: How does an ABG separate PE from hyperventilation syndrome?
cards.back: Both show respiratory alkalosis; PaO2 is **low in PE** and high in hyperventilation

cards.front: Two-level Wells cut-off for PE and what follows?
cards.back: **Over 4 = likely** → CTPA. **4 or less = unlikely** → D-dimer, CTPA only if raised

cards.front: When is a V/Q scan chosen instead of CTPA?
cards.back: Contrast allergy or renal impairment (also to limit breast radiation); best with a normal CXR

cards.front: Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off?
cards.back: 500 below age 50; **10 × age** from 50 years

cards.front: Commonest ECG finding in PE?
cards.back: **Sinus tachycardia**; S1Q3T3 is uncommon

cards.front: Hampton hump vs Westermark sign?
cards.back: Hampton hump: wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity (infarct). Westermark: oligaemia beyond the clot

cards.front: Six items of the simplified PESI?
cards.back: Age over 80, cancer, chronic heart/lung disease, pulse 110 or more, systolic BP under 100, SaO2 under 90%

cards.front: Definition of high-risk (massive) PE?
cards.back: Shock, arrest or systolic BP **under 90 mmHg** (or a fall over 40 mmHg for over 15 min) not due to another cause

cards.front: Definite indication for thrombolysis in PE?
cards.back: Acute massive PE with **cardiogenic shock / persistent hypotension**

cards.front: Indications for an IVC filter (Davidson)?
cards.back: Anticoagulation contraindicated, massive bleeding on it, or recurrent VTE despite it

cards.front: Which DOACs can be started without LMWH?
cards.back: **Rivaroxaban** (high dose 21 days) and **apixaban** (high dose 7 days); dabigatran and edoxaban need 5 days of LMWH first

cards.front: When can LMWH stop after starting warfarin?
cards.back: After at least 5 days **and** INR over 2 (on 2 consecutive days)

cards.front: Anticoagulant for PE in pregnancy?
cards.back: **LMWH**; warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs cross the placenta

cards.front: What is CTEPH and how can it be cured?
cards.back: Persistent pulmonary hypertension from unresolved emboli (up to 5%); **pulmonary endarterectomy** in selected patients

cards.front: Recurrence risk after unprovoked VTE?
cards.back: About **7–10% per year**, reaching 30–40% at 5 years

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man who injects drugs has fevers and a vegetation on his tricuspid valve on echo. Chest X-ray shows several new nodular shadows in both lungs.
items.explanation: Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis seeds the lungs with infected emboli.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is breathless and confused 2 days after a femoral shaft fracture. He has a petechial rash.
items.explanation: Two steps: the timing after a long-bone fracture and the petechial rash with confusion point away from thrombus and towards fat embolism.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman collapses with sudden breathlessness and hypotension minutes after a vaginal delivery.
items.explanation: Sudden collapse around delivery fits amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man 9 days after a hip replacement has sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness. His operated thigh is swollen and tender.
items.explanation: Most PEs come from proximal leg DVT, and major lower-limb orthopaedic surgery is a strong risk factor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman, 10 days after a knee replacement, suddenly becomes breathless and faint. She is cold, cyanosed and her BP is 82/50 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: Which other finding best indicates that this is a massive rather than a small PE?
options: Raised JVP with a right ventricular gallop
questions.explanation: Massive PE causes acute right heart failure with a low output: hypotension, a raised JVP and an RV gallop. The other features belong to a smaller, peripheral embolus that has infarcted lung.
whyNot: A rub signals peripheral infarction, typical of small or medium PE.
Haemoptysis follows lung infarction from a smaller embolus.
Low-grade fever accompanies infarction from a small or medium PE.
Pleuritic pain comes from a peripheral infarct touching the pleura.

questions.stem: In a large study of patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism, symptoms were recorded at presentation.
questions.leadIn: Which symptom was the most common?
questions.explanation: Breathlessness is the commonest symptom of PE (about three-quarters in PIOPED); tachypnoea is the commonest sign.
whyNot: Haemoptysis occurs in only about 1 in 8 patients.
Syncope suggests a massive PE and is uncommon.
Wheeze occurs in about a fifth.
Orthopnoea occurs in about a quarter.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman becomes acutely breathless after an argument. ABG on air: pH 7.51, PaCO2 3.5 kPa, PaO2 14.1 kPa. Her chest X-ray is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: respiratory alkalosis fits both PE and hyperventilation, but the high PaO2 favours hyperventilation; PE lowers the PaO2.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman on the combined pill has pleuritic chest pain 10 days after a long-haul flight. Pulse is 112/min, SpO2 90% on air, and the chest X-ray is clear.
items.explanation: Risk factors plus hypoxaemia with a normal chest film should prompt imaging for PE.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden, tearing central chest pain that goes through to his back.
items.explanation: Tearing pain radiating to the back is the classic description of aortic dissection, one of the key mimics of massive PE.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has sharp left chest pain on breathing after lifting furniture. Pressing on one costal cartilage reproduces the pain exactly; observations are normal.
items.explanation: Pain reproduced by local pressure with normal observations suggests a musculoskeletal cause.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has mild pleuritic pain. Pulse is 104/min; there are no other risk factors or leg signs, and another diagnosis seems more likely than PE.
items.explanation: Wells score 1.5 (heart rate only), so PE is unlikely; a D-dimer is the next step.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has brief pleuritic pain and one episode of blood-streaked sputum. Her Wells score is 1 and a sensitive D-dimer is normal.
items.explanation: A low Wells score plus a normal sensitive D-dimer excludes PE without imaging.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has a swollen, tender calf and acute breathlessness; PE is the most likely diagnosis. He had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast last year. His chest X-ray is normal.
items.explanation: Wells over 4 means imaging is needed. Contrast allergy rules out CTPA, and a normal chest film makes a V/Q scan likely to be diagnostic.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has a swollen, tender left leg and pleuritic pain; PE is the leading diagnosis. Renal function is normal.
items.explanation: Wells score at least 6 (DVT signs 3 plus PE most likely 3), so go straight to CTPA without a D-dimer.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a confirmed PE has a 12-lead ECG.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most likely ECG finding?
questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG abnormality in PE. The other changes reflect right heart strain from larger clots and are much less frequent.
whyNot: S1Q3T3 is the textbook pattern but is uncommon, even in massive PE.
RBBB occurs with larger emboli but is not the usual finding.
New AF can occur but is less common than sinus tachycardia.
P pulmonale is an occasional strain sign.

questions.stem: A chest X-ray in a patient with proven PE shows a wedge-shaped opacity based on the pleura at the right base.
questions.leadIn: What is this sign called?
questions.explanation: A pleural-based wedge of opacity marks pulmonary infarction (Hampton hump). It is a classic but uncommon sign.
whyNot: Westermark sign is oligaemia beyond the clot, a lucent area, not an opacity.
A deep sulcus sign suggests pneumothorax on a supine film.
Kerley B lines indicate interstitial oedema.
Air bronchograms point to consolidation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD has a confirmed PE. Pulse is 115/min, BP 112/70 mmHg and SaO2 92% on air. He has no cancer or heart failure.
questions.leadIn: What is his simplified PESI score?
questions.explanation: He scores 1 for chronic lung disease and 1 for a pulse of 110 or more. Age is under 80, BP is not below 100 and SaO2 is not below 90%. A score of 1 or more means he is not low risk.
whyNot: A score of 0 ignores both his COPD and his heart rate.
Only one of his two positive items has been counted.
His age, BP and saturation do not reach the thresholds.
Only two items are positive.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with PE has BP 128/76 mmHg. Echo shows a dilated right ventricle and her troponin is raised. sPESI is 1.
questions.leadIn: What is her risk class?
questions.explanation: She is normotensive, so not high risk. With sPESI 1 or more and both RV dysfunction and a raised troponin, she is intermediate-high risk and needs close monitoring for decompensation.
whyNot: High risk needs shock or persistent hypotension.
Intermediate-low has one or neither marker; she has both.
Low risk needs sPESI 0 with normal RV and troponin.
This is an acute presentation, not chronic disease.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with a CT-proven large PE has BP 76/40 mmHg despite fluids. She has no bleeding history.
items.explanation: Massive PE with shock is the definite indication for thrombolysis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man had a craniotomy 6 days ago. He now has a massive PE with BP 70/40 mmHg.
items.explanation: Two steps: shock calls for reperfusion, but recent intracranial surgery contraindicates lysis, so surgical embolectomy is the option.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with acute proximal DVT and a stable PE is bleeding actively from a duodenal ulcer.
items.explanation: Anticoagulation is contraindicated, so a retrievable filter protects him until it can start.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a small PE has sPESI 0, a normal RV on CT, a normal troponin and good support at home.
items.explanation: Low-risk PE can be treated as an outpatient, and apixaban can be used alone from day 1.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant has a confirmed PE.
items.explanation: LMWH does not cross the placenta; warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs cross the placenta.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man on day 8 of LMWH for PE has a platelet count that has fallen from 260 to 110 × 10⁹/L, with a new thrombosis.
items.explanation: Two steps: a fall of over 50% after 5–14 days of heparin means HIT; stop all heparin and use a non-heparin agent such as argatroban.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome has a new PE and normal renal function.
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an indication for warfarin rather than a DOAC, started with parenteral cover.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with massive PE and BP 80/50 mmHg is being assessed for thrombolysis.
items.explanation: IV unfractionated heparin is preferred when lysis or catheter therapy is being considered, because it can be stopped quickly.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man had a large PE 8 months ago and completed anticoagulation. He remains breathless on exertion. He has a loud P2, echo shows raised pulmonary pressures and a perfusion scan shows persistent defects.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment offers a possible cure?
questions.explanation: Persistent breathlessness, pulmonary hypertension and residual perfusion defects after PE indicate CTEPH. Pulmonary endarterectomy can cure selected patients.
whyNot: Lysis treats fresh clot, not organised chronic thrombus.
A filter does not remove existing obstruction.
Embolectomy is for acute massive PE.
Stockings are for leg symptoms, not pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A review of deaths from bleeding in patients taking warfarin for VTE is carried out.
questions.leadIn: Which bleeding site is the commonest cause of death?
questions.explanation: Intracerebral haemorrhage is the commonest cause of fatal bleeding on warfarin.
whyNot: GI bleeding is common but less often fatal.
Retroperitoneal bleeding is less common.
Pulmonary haemorrhage is rare.
Haematuria is rarely fatal.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman, 3 weeks after knee surgery, coughs up a small amount of blood with sudden right pleuritic pain. A pleural rub is heard and her temperature is 37.7 °C.
items.explanation: Recent surgery, sudden pleuritic pain, haemoptysis and a rub fit pulmonary infarction from PE; low-grade fever is common.

items.stem: A 71-year-old heavy smoker has coughed up small streaks of blood in his sputum on and off for 2 months. He has no fever or night sweats.
items.explanation: Repeated small haemoptysis or blood-streaked sputum strongly suggests lung cancer, and smoking is its main cause. Without fever or night sweats, TB is less likely.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man wakes at night severely breathless and coughing pink, frothy sputum.
items.explanation: Pink frothy sputum is typical of pulmonary oedema.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has coughed up large daily volumes of green sputum for years and now has recurrent haemoptysis.
items.explanation: Copious purulent sputum over years points to bronchiectasis.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has 2 days of fever, rigors and rust-coloured sputum, with bronchial breathing at the left base.
items.explanation: Rusty sputum with fever and consolidation suggests pneumococcal pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a massive PE has BP 84/52 mmHg, a raised JVP and a dilated right ventricle on echo. He is awaiting thrombolysis.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Diuretics and vasodilators reduce cardiac output in a failing, preload-dependent right ventricle and should be avoided.
whyNot: Fluids help raise filling pressure in shock from PE.
Oxygen should keep SaO2 above 90%.
UFH is the preferred anticoagulant when lysis is planned.
Opiates can relieve pain and distress if used cautiously.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman has a swollen right calf and sudden breathlessness; PE is the most likely diagnosis. Her Wells score is 6. A D-dimer sent from triage is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: With PE likely (Wells over 4), D-dimer should not be used to exclude it. She needs imaging, and CTPA is first-line.
whyNot: A normal D-dimer only excludes PE when probability is low.
Repeating the test does not address the high pre-test probability.
Aspirin is not treatment for VTE.
An outpatient echo delays diagnosis and cannot exclude PE.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with PE is started on LMWH and warfarin on the same day.
questions.leadIn: When can the LMWH be stopped?
options: After at least 5 days and once the INR is over 2
As soon as the first INR reaches 1.5
questions.explanation: Warfarin takes days to work fully, so LMWH continues for at least 5 days and until the INR is over 2 (on 2 consecutive days).
whyNot: 48 hours is too short; warfarin is not yet therapeutic.
An INR of 1.5 is below the target range of 2–3.
Warfarin needs at least 5 days to anticoagulate fully, so on its own it gives no early protection.
Three months is the usual total duration, not the overlap.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man completes 6 months of anticoagulation for unprovoked PE and asks about his chance of recurrence.
questions.leadIn: Which pair of factors most strongly predicts recurrence?
options: Female sex and a normal D-dimer after stopping
Male sex and a raised D-dimer 1 month after stopping
Age under 40 and a distal DVT
Recent surgery as the trigger and a normal echo
questions.explanation: After unprovoked VTE, male sex and a positive D-dimer one month after stopping anticoagulation are the strongest predictors of recurrence.
whyNot: Women recur less, and a normal D-dimer is reassuring.
Distal DVT carries a lower recurrence risk.
A surgical trigger means provoked VTE with lower recurrence.
These are weak risk factors for a first event, not strong recurrence predictors.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman had a hysterectomy 2 weeks ago. She now has sudden breathlessness and coughed up a little blood. Pulse is 108/min. Her legs are normal, and the team thinks PE is more likely than any other diagnosis.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Step 1, Wells score: PE most likely (3) + surgery within 4 weeks (1.5) + heart rate over 100 (1.5) + haemoptysis (1) = 7. Step 2: over 4 means PE is **likely**. Step 3: when PE is likely, skip the D-dimer and image directly; CTPA is first-line and can also show an alternative diagnosis.
whyNot: A D-dimer is only used when PE is unlikely (Wells 4 or less).
With no leg signs, a normal leg scan would not exclude PE.
An exercise ECG does not test for PE and could be dangerous.
Waiting delays the diagnosis of a treatable, potentially fatal condition.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with sudden breathlessness. ABG on air: pH 7.48, PaCO2 3.9 kPa, PaO2 8.1 kPa, with a widened A–a gradient.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis best fits this gas?
questions.explanation: Step 1: high pH with low PaCO2 means respiratory alkalosis. Step 2: two common causes are PE and hyperventilation. Step 3: PaO2 is **low** with a raised A–a gradient, which fits PE (dead space and mismatch); hyperventilation gives a high PaO2.
whyNot: Hyperventilation drives the PaO2 up, not down.
COPD type 2 failure has a raised PaCO2.
DKA causes a metabolic acidosis with a low pH.
Opioid overdose causes hypoventilation with a high PaCO2.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man collapses at home 2 weeks after a long-haul flight. In the emergency department his BP is 78/45 mmHg after a fluid bolus. CT is not available at once, and bedside echo shows a dilated, poorly moving right ventricle with a small, vigorous left ventricle. He has had no recent surgery, bleeding or stroke.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Step 1: persistent shock means high-risk (massive) PE. Step 2: when CTPA is not immediately available, echo evidence of RV overload in an unstable patient is enough to justify PE-specific treatment. Step 3: shock is the definite indication for thrombolysis, and he has no contraindication. Had lysis been contraindicated (e.g. surgery within 14 days), surgical embolectomy would be the alternative.
whyNot: LMWH alone does not relieve the obstruction causing shock.
Diuretics lower output and worsen shock.
A filter prevents new emboli but does nothing for the current one.
An oral agent is far too slow for a shocked patient.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has pleuritic pain and a swollen, tender left calf.
items.explanation: In pregnancy, compression ultrasound of the legs can come first; a proximal DVT allows treatment without chest imaging.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman on ICU after a hip fracture repair is suddenly hypotensive and hypoxaemic. She is too unstable to move to the scanner.
items.explanation: Bedside echo showing RV dilatation or clot in transit supports PE in a patient too unstable for CT.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has a Wells score of 2. His D-dimer comes back raised.
items.explanation: PE is unlikely, but a raised D-dimer means imaging is required; CTPA is first-line.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COPD and bullous lungs has a Wells score of 6. His renal function is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: imaging is needed, and a V/Q scan is often non-diagnostic with chronic lung disease, so CTPA is better.

questions.theme: Complications of PE and its treatment
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman on day 10 of LMWH has a platelet count that has fallen from 300 to 120 × 10⁹/L and a new DVT in the other leg.
items.explanation: A fall of more than half in platelets 5–14 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis, is HIT.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with protein C deficiency starts warfarin without heparin cover. On day 3 she develops painful, darkening patches on her thighs.
items.explanation: Skin necrosis is a warfarin side effect in people with protein C or S deficiency, and it appears soon after treatment starts.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man had a permanent IVC filter placed a year ago. He now has swelling of both legs.
items.explanation: Two steps: bilateral rather than one-sided swelling suggests a central cause; filter thrombosis obstructs the IVC.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man had a proximal femoral DVT 2 years ago. His leg now aches and swells by evening, and he has an ulcer above the medial malleolus.
items.explanation: Valve damage after proximal DVT causes post-thrombotic syndrome; ulceration near the medial malleolus is its severest form.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had LMWH throughout pregnancy for PE. Shortly after delivery she has a vertebral fracture after minor strain.
items.explanation: Long-term heparin use can cause osteoporosis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant needs chest imaging for suspected PE after a normal leg ultrasound. She asks how CTPA compares with a V/Q scan.
questions.leadIn: Which statement is correct?
options: CTPA gives the fetus less radiation but gives the breast more
CTPA gives both fetus and breast less radiation
V/Q gives the fetus less radiation and the breast more
Neither test may be used in pregnancy
questions.explanation: CTPA delivers a lower fetal dose (0.01–0.06 mGy) than V/Q (0.11–0.22 mGy) but more to maternal breast tissue.
whyNot: CTPA gives more breast radiation, not less.
This is the wrong way round.
The doses differ meaningfully.
Both are used; VTE is a leading cause of maternal death.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has massive PE with BP 80/45 mmHg. Thrombolysis is being considered.
questions.leadIn: Which feature in his history is a contraindication?
questions.explanation: GI bleeding within the previous 21 days contraindicates fibrinolysis.
whyNot: Age alone is not a contraindication.
The threshold is above 180/110 mmHg.
The surgical exclusion window is 14 days.
The INR threshold is above 1.7.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Small or medium PE with lung infarction

items.stem: A 42-year-old man, 3 weeks into a below-knee cast, has left pleuritic pain, a little haemoptysis, a pleural rub and a temperature of 37.6 °C. His chest X-ray shows a raised left hemidiaphragm and a small effusion that is blood-stained on tapping.
items.explanation: Two steps: the fever and rub could suggest pneumonia, but immobilisation, haemoptysis, a raised diaphragm and a blood-stained effusion point to infarction from a small or medium PE.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a DVT 2 years ago has 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness. She has an RV heave and a loud P2; her chest X-ray shows enlarged pulmonary arteries.
items.explanation: Slowly progressive breathlessness with signs of pulmonary hypertension after VTE suggests chronic thromboembolic disease.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man collapses 8 days after hip fracture surgery. BP is 75/40 mmHg. Echo shows a dilated right ventricle, a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle and thrombus in the RV outflow tract.
items.explanation: Post-operative collapse with an under-filled vigorous LV, a dilated RV and visible clot in the outflow tract is massive PE.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has a second PE despite a therapeutic INR on warfarin, confirmed on several checks.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which is an accepted indication for an IVC filter?
options: A first unprovoked PE in a stable patient
Proximal DVT in a patient able to take apixaban
Low-risk PE managed as an outpatient
Intermediate-high risk PE already on heparin
questions.explanation: Davidson lists three indications: anticoagulation contraindicated, massive bleeding on anticoagulation, and recurrent VTE despite anticoagulation. Filters add nothing for routine patients who can be anticoagulated.
whyNot: Routine anticoagulation is enough; a filter adds risk without benefit.
He can be anticoagulated, so no filter is needed.
Low-risk patients need anticoagulation only.
A filter does not treat the acute embolus or replace monitoring.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer on chemotherapy is diagnosed with PE.
questions.leadIn: In this setting, which maintenance anticoagulant has a lower recurrence rate than warfarin?
questions.explanation: In active cancer, maintenance LMWH gives fewer recurrences than warfarin. DOACs may be as effective but cause more bleeding.
whyNot: Aspirin is not adequate VTE treatment.
Filters do not prevent recurrence on their own and raise DVT risk.
A long-term IV infusion is impractical and not standard.
Active cancer carries a very high recurrence risk.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has his first PE with no identifiable trigger. He is stable and has a low bleeding risk.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?
options: 3 months, then stop in every case
At least 3 months, then usually continue long term
Lifelong warfarin at INR 3–4 plus an IVC filter
questions.explanation: Unprovoked VTE recurs at 7–10% per year after stopping. Treat for at least 3 months, then usually continue; NICE advises offering long-term anticoagulation after unprovoked PE.
whyNot: Six weeks is too short for a proximal PE.
Stopping at 3 months suits provoked VTE with a removed trigger.
A higher INR target and a filter add bleeding and device risks without benefit.
Aspirin does not replace anticoagulation.

ospe.identify: Chest X-ray features of PE and infarction: wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity, raised hemidiaphragm, basal linear shadows, small effusion, oligaemic zone, enlarged pulmonary artery.
ECG of acute PE: sinus tachycardia, S wave in I, Q wave and inverted T in III (S1Q3T3), incomplete RBBB.
CT pulmonary angiogram: filling defect (saddle embolus) across the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery.
CTPA at the level of the main pulmonary arteries: large filling defect (thrombus) in the left pulmonary artery.
V/Q scan: ventilation preserved but perfusion absent in the right upper lobe, a mismatched defect that indicates PE.
